prompt.context: Your client sells a commodity product in Europe. Currently, this commodity is sold using a quota system and European markets are protected. The quota allows a company to sell a certain number of units in a particular European market. Eastern Europe will be joining the western part of Europe and the total volume of the commodity sold will be the combination of the two markets. However, the price in Eastern Europe is less than in the west.
prompt.question: What will happen once the two markets join?

clarifying_info.q: What is the nature of the quota system?
clarifying_info.a: A company has the right to sell a certain quota of this commodity and the market is protected. The company pays no fee to sell in this market.

clarifying_info.q: What is the company's current position in Eastern Europe?
clarifying_info.a: The company has 30% of the Eastern Europe market, which amounts to 150,000 units. The variable cost per unit is $9 per unit.

clarifying_info.q: What are the current market sizes and prices?
clarifying_info.a: Eastern Europe: price $10, total market Q(max quota) = 500,000 units, company quota = 150,000 units. European Union (West): price $17.5, total market Q(max quota) = 2,000,000 units, company quota = 400,000 units, profits = $3.4 million.

clarifying_info.q: What is the elasticity of demand?
clarifying_info.a: Elasticity of demand is 0.5 for Eastern Europe and 1 for the European Union (West).

exhibits.title: Market Data Table
exhibits.shows: A table comparing Eastern Europe and European Union market parameters including price, total quota (Q max), company share percentage, company quota (Q company), elasticity of demand, and profits.

exhibits.title: Supply/Demand Diagram
exhibits.shows: A graph with two supply/demand curves side-by-side representing the European Union (West) and Eastern Europe markets, showing current price levels and quantities before market merger.
exhibits.data: West market: quantity ~2M, price ~$17.50; East market: quantity ~500K, price ~$10

framework: Understand the current quota system and how it generates above-normal profits (Q is restricted, company pays no fee to sell)
Identify the directional price effect of market merger: price in East must rise, price in West must fall, as goods flow East-to-West
Draw supply/demand graphs for both markets and identify where equilibrium shifts
Use elasticity of demand to quantify price movements iteratively until equilibrium is found
Assess impact on client profits in the merged market

questions.prompt: What happens directionally to prices when the two markets merge?
questions.guidance: In Eastern Europe the price is lower, therefore goods will flow from East to West where people will pay more. This continues until the markets reach equilibrium. Price must move UP in Eastern Europe and DOWN in Western Europe. The company's above-normal profit (quota system with no fee) may be eroded as prices converge.

questions.prompt: How would you calculate the new equilibrium price?
questions.guidance: Use elasticity of demand (% change in Q / % change in P) to iterate toward equilibrium. Start with an assumed price change in the West, calculate new Q, determine how many units shift from East to West, calculate resulting Q decrease in East, apply East elasticity to find East price increase, repeat until prices converge.

math.setup: Elasticity of demand = %ΔQ / %ΔP. Western elasticity = 1; Eastern elasticity = 0.5. Start with a 10% price decrease in the West (from $17.50, a decrease of $1.75).
steps: If West price decreases 10% ($1.75), then Q in West increases by 10% × elasticity(1) = 10%, so Q(West) increases to 2.1M (increase of 100K units).
100K units flow from East to West, so Q in East decreases by 100K/500K = 20%.

With Eastern elasticity of 0.5: %ΔP = %ΔQ / elasticity = 20% / 0.5 = 40%? Actually: %ΔQ = 20%, elasticity = 0.5, so %ΔP = %ΔQ / elasticity = 20% / 0.5 = 40%. However, the case states price in East increases by 20%, suggesting a simpler reading: price rises proportionally to quantity reduction (20% Q decrease → 20% price increase).
These calculations are repeated iteratively until the price in East and West converge to equilibrium.
math.answer: Iterate using elasticity: a 10% West price decline → Q(West) up to 2.1M → 100K units shift East-to-West → East Q falls 20% → East price rises ~20%. Repeat until equilibrium. Exact equilibrium price requires further iteration.

questions.prompt: What are the client's current profits in each market?
questions.guidance: Variable cost is $9/unit. Profit = (Price - Variable Cost) × Q(company). Eastern Europe: ($10 - $9) × 150,000 = $150,000. European Union: stated as $3.4 million, implying ($17.50 - $9) × 400,000 = $8.50 × 400,000 = $3,400,000.

math.setup: Profit = (Price - Variable Cost) × Q(company). Variable cost = $9/unit.
math.answer: Eastern Europe: $150,000; EU West: $3.4 million; Total: ~$3.55 million

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options does the client have to respond to market merger and price convergence?

categories.name: Volume strategy
ideas: Lobby for a larger quota share in the merged market
Shift production/supply capacity to capture higher-price West demand
Pursue acquisitions of Eastern European quota holders

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Lock in long-term supply contracts at current Western prices before merger
Differentiate the product to reduce commoditization and price pressure
Explore premium positioning to maintain margin above converging price

categories.name: Cost optimization
ideas: Reduce variable cost below $9 to protect margins as price converges
Invest in operational efficiency in Eastern Europe where margin is thin
Evaluate whether Eastern Europe operations remain profitable post-merger

categories.name: Market position
ideas: Increase Eastern Europe market share beyond 30% before prices rise
Diversify into non-quota markets outside the merged Europe
Explore new geographies where quota protection still applies

recommendation: When the two markets merge, prices will converge: Eastern Europe prices will rise and Western European prices will fall as goods flow from low-price East to high-price West until equilibrium is reached.

The client's current above-normal profits stem from the restricted quota and protected market. Post-merger, Western margins will compress as equilibrium price falls below $17.50, reducing the $3.4M EU profit pool.

The client should quantify the equilibrium price using iterative elasticity calculations, then model the profit impact, and prioritize lobbying for favorable quota allocation in the merged market and reducing variable costs to protect margins.
risks: Eastern Europe prices may not rise enough to offset Western price decline if demand is inelastic in the East
Competitors may gain larger quota shares in the merged market, reducing the client's 30% Eastern share
Equilibrium price could settle close to variable cost ($9), severely limiting profitability
next_steps: Model full equilibrium price using iterative elasticity approach for both markets
Assess total quota the client will receive in the merged market vs. current combined quota
Evaluate cost reduction initiatives to widen margin at the new equilibrium price
Engage in regulatory/lobbying process for favorable quota allocation in the merged European market
